text: Your bank card has no battery. No charger, no switch. Yet every time you tap it, it wakes up, does secret maths, and goes back to sleep. In under a second.
So where does the power come from? The answer is the same trick that charges your electric toothbrush.
Hidden under the plastic, a thin wire loops around the edge of the card. Again, and again, and again.
The card reader is always humming an invisible magnetic field. It flips direction about thirteen million times a second.
Bring your card close, and that flipping field pushes electricity around the loop. No contact at all. Just like the toothbrush on its stand.
A tiny chip wakes up on that borrowed power. It only works a few centimetres away. That's why you have to get so close.
And here's the weird part. To answer, the card doesn't even transmit. It just flickers how much power it takes, and the reader feels the pattern. Like blinking a torch in morse code.
Now the clever bit. The chip holds a secret key that never, ever leaves it.
For every tap, it mixes that key with the amount, a counter, and a random number, into a one time code.
The bank checks the code. It matches? Paid. Beep.
So what if a thief secretly records your tap? They get a code that's already been used. Try it again, and the bank just says no.
No battery. No contact. Just a loop of wire, borrowed power, and a code that only works once.
Orbi Transfer was built on the same idea. Your file is locked on your own phone, with a code that never leaves it.
It only shows up on screens near you. Twelve wrong guesses, and it locks itself. Thirty minutes later, it's gone.
Orbi Transfer dot com. Now you know what happens in every tap.
